Viv the Violin

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Commission

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
FINDING VIV
On her tenth birthday, Diana Neille is given a violin by her father, a gift that carries weight long before its meaning is fully understood, because to raise a violinist is to endure years of unmelodious sound, the scrape of bow on string that can feel like chalk dragged across a school board, demanding patience before it offers anything like beauty in return.
Diana practises, she plays in eisteddfods, and slowly, through the accumulation of hours and repetition, the violin settles into her body, becoming part of her muscle memory, something held instinctively between chin and shoulder, a physical extension through which her musical voice reaches the world. She names the violin Viv.
Then, twelve years ago, Viv disappears, stolen during a house robbery at a moment when Diana’s life is already unsettled. At the police station, the charge office is full of people reporting hijackings, assaults and murders, and it feels almost impossible to explain that what has been taken is a violin, an object that is deeply personal but difficult to place alongside the violence surrounding it.
Instead of persisting there, Diana turns elsewhere, appealing to a different kind of authority, the diffuse reach of the internet. She creates a Facebook page and writes that she has lost what feels like a limb, a violin she calls Viv, carefully listing every identifying detail she can remember. One detail matters more than the rest: the bridge was hand carved by her violin teacher and mentor, Bernard Wozny, a respected luthier who signs his bridges and stamps his name into the wood.
And then she waits.
Days turn into months, months into years, and eventually more than a decade passes with no response. Diana buys another violin, one that does the job but never quite feels right, its sound unfamiliar, its weight slightly off, and playing becomes effort rather than instinct. Over time, the sharpness of the loss fades, and Diana moves away from music making and into film making, carrying the memory of Viv quietly rather than actively.
Recently, at supper, Diana’s niece tells her that she has started learning the violin, and Diana says she wishes she could have passed Viv down to her. If this were a piece of music, this would be the long pause, a rest held in the score.
Not long after that pause, Diana receives a message from a stranger called Kyle, who says he thinks he may have her violin.
At this point the story shifts, becoming a kind of whodunnit told in reverse. How did the violin survive? Where has it been all this time? Who handled it, and how did it make its way back?
Kyle explains that while cataloguing his collection of instruments and music memorabilia, he noticed a name carved into a violin bridge. Curious, he searched it, and the old Facebook page appeared. He tells Diana that he bought a large collection of instruments from a friend who emigrated overseas, and that among them was this violin, which his friend had bought years earlier from a Cash Converters in Johannesburg, shortly after the original robbery.
Kyle is an unlikely detective. Formerly a data analyst, now a devoted collector of musical objects, his tastes are eclectic rather than classical, his house filled with instruments and memorabilia gathered for love rather than profit. He meets Diana at a Woolworths, and when he walks in, he is carrying the case. Inside it is Viv.
When the violin is found, Diana contacts her former teacher, Bernard Wozny, the man who carved and signed the bridge that ultimately solved the mystery. Bernard is now in his eighties, recently weakened by a stroke that has forced him to give up his workshop and pass his tools on to a younger luthier, Albertus Bakkes. There is another unresolved thread here too: Bernard’s own home was robbed not long ago, and several violins he had restored were stolen and never recovered.
Viv is taken to see him. Bernard recognises the instrument immediately, not by its sound, but by the bridge.
The question that remains is simple and unanswered: how many more stories like this are still sitting quietly in cases, waiting for the right detail to be noticed.


Further information:
PEOPLE TO INTERVIEW
Diana Neille – musician and filmmaker, owner of the stolen violin
Kyle Fenton – the collector who identified and returned the instrument
Bernard Wozny – violin teacher and luthier who carved and signed the bridge
Albertus Bakkes – contemporary luthier now caring for the instrument and inheriting the tools and knowledge of the craft
FORMAT AND STYLE
A 10 to 12 minute Carte Blanche feature, structured as a gentle whodunnit, unfolding backwards through clues embedded in wood, memory and digital traces, led by narrative rather than exposition, with music and sound carrying the investigation forward.

(Diana) So this is the A string. I know do. Have you watched an orchestra before?
(Masa) I have.
(Diana) So, the oboe will play an A. They’ll play a nice long note. And then you’ll hear everyone tune to that same note. To make sure that everybody is in tune together. Otherwise, it will sound terrible.
( Masa) Diana Neille comes from a musical family.
She has been tuning and re-tuning her violin since the age of five.
(Diana) What kind of music do you like, then I can play it for you?
(Masa) I like classical music, I like jazz music.

(Diana) Do you know this one?
(Masa) A memorable moment: Music brought to life by a remarkable musician, and a violin with a story of its own.
(Masa) How long did you take to become good at it?
(Diana) I was playing in public by about 8 or 9. My sister and I had a standing gig at the Hyde Park Mall, we’d play at the movies every Friday.
My sister would put my hair up in pig tails and make me look extra cute and like pinch my cheeks and stuff. To try and make people feel sorry for me or like, you know, here’s these little girls playing their instruments. So no, we killed it, we did, we slayed, we made a lot of money.
(Masa) When it became clear that Diana was serious about music, her father decided to invest.Her teacher, Bernard Wozny, was not only a conductor but also a luthier, someone who works on violins. One of the instruments he restored was a 135-year-old French violin, which Diana’s father bought for her.
(Bernard) That instrument comes from Mirecourt, they made violins for 300 years up to now. So when I worked on the violin and I started to play, it was amazing how fantastic the violin sound.
(Masa) This violin became central to her life. It took her from playing with ensembles, to performing Beethoven’s Ninth, in New York’s, Carnegie Hall.


(Diana) You know, it was a big deal, because it’s an old instrument, it’s a very good instrument with a beautiful sound. And I called her Viv, just ‘cause it short for violin I guess. It just seemed to fit.
(Masa) Twelve years ago, Diana’s house was burgled. The kind that happens every day. The burglars took what they could carry. And amongst the items, was Viv the violin.
(Diana) I came back and the front door was open, and just the whole place was in disarray.
(Masa) After more than ten years together, losing Viv was heartbreaking.
(Diana) It was the weirdest feeling, you know that something is, so much a part of your life. It really feels like losing a limb or a….ja, it’s, it’s a big deal.”
(Albertus) When an instrument like that is lost you know, it can be almost like losing a loved one.”
(Masa) Albertus Bekker is a luthier in Linden, Johannesburg, who inherited many of Bernard Wozny’s tools when he retired.
(Masa) Do people steal violins? Is that a thing?
(Albertus) Ja. People read about these famous violins and millions of dollars value, and, when they see an old violin, the temptation is there to, to, nick it.”
(Masa) Albertus says that when a rare instrument is stolen, finding a legitimate buyer is extremely difficult.
(Albertus) What you’ll often find is the perpetrator tries to get rid of it as quickly as possible and it ends up in the nearest pawn shop or antique shop.
(Masa) After the theft, Diana went to the police, checked pawn shops and antique dealers, doing everything she could to find Viv.
(Diana) I’d sort of had to give up the search. And so, you know, I did what anyone would do in twenty, what was it twenty, end of 2013, I made a facebook page, in the hopes that someone would you know come across it, you never know right.”
(Masa) But no one ever came forward, and as the years passed without any news, the trail eventually went cold.
With the insurance payout, Diana bought a new violin, but it never became part of her in quite the same way.
(Diana) It’s difficult to explain. I took joy out of being with other people and the privilege of playing with other people and making music and making people happy and making people dance. But I didn’t enjoy playing.
(Influence Documentary) This is a whole new political landscape which has no geographical borders.
(Masa) Resigned to the idea that she would never see Viv again, Diana moved on, building a new career as a journalist and filmmaker. Then, earlier this year, there was an unexpected development. Kyle Fenton is an avid collector, with dozens of musical instruments in his care.
(Kyle) I play the drums, I play the piano, the keyboard, ukulele, base guitar.
(Masa) Geez that’s a lot, anything else?”
(Kyle) If it makes a noise I give it a go. Laughs.
(Masa) Kyle’s friend shared his passion for collecting all things musical.
(Kyle) We had a lot more money than brains when we were younger and we would scour all the different second hand shops, buying music instruments for next to nothing, that were actually quite valuable.
(Masa) In 2013, they spotted a unique violin in a second hand shop.
(Kyle) I bought the violin hoping to learn how to play one, but it was just a bit too complicated for me.
(Masa) So Kyle packed it away in the roof, where it stayed for seven years. Until two months ago. When Kyle finally took it out, he noticed something he had missed before. A small signature on the bridge. The name: B Wozny.
(Masa) This small piece of wood is the bridge. It holds the strings and it carries the sound into the body of the violin. Now years ago, when Bernard Wozny was working on Diana’s instrument, he made a new bridge and, as he always did, he signed it.
(Masa) Kyle set out to find Bernard Wozny.

(Masa) 12 years is a long time on-line and posts like Diana’s sink out of sight. Most people would never be able to find them again.

(Masa) After hours online, Kyle finally tracked down the post.
And suddenly, the pieces began to fall into place.
Once he was sure, he made contact. “Amongst a small fortune of instruments I purchased, I discovered I have, in my possession, one 4/4, H Clotelle violin in pristine condition for its age… with markings on the bridge piece which read, B. Wozny.”
(Diana) I read it and before I even finished it, I , you know, I got so excited. And I was with a friend at the time, and she came running and she’s like what’s wrong, why are you screaming.
(Masa) They agreed to meet the next day.
(Diana) I was so nervous, just waiting for him to walk in the door and he did, and he’s carrying, my old, I could see my old ratty case.”
(Kyle) And she stood up, an I walked up to her and I handed her the violin and I said to her, I believe this belongs to you. And she puts it down, she just looked at me and I could see the tear run down her face.
(Kyle) And when she opened it, she just started to shake.
(Diana) Ja, it was, it was incredible.
You know I think especially now, we just dealing with so much, the world is in such a crazy place. Where it just feels like you are being bombarded with bad news. And it was just this incredibly sweet, and improbable, unlikely story.
(Masa) It seemed fitting for Diana to take Viv back to see Bernard, the man whose signature had brought the violin home.
(Bernard) It’s my pride,to,to, that she has the instrument and she’s young and healthy and that she can still perform.
(Masa) Bernard says Viv’s return is a miracle. He’s still hoping that seven of his own violins, stolen years ago, will find their way home.

(Kyle) I’d managed to bring a little bit of light into her life and I am glad I did.
And it was never mine to begin, so it must go home to where she truly belongs.
(Masa) And before I go, just enough time for a quick encore.
(Masa) Bravo, bravo, I love it.

And suddenly, the pieces began to fall into place. Once he was sure, he made contact. “Amongst a small fortune of instruments I purchased, I discovered I have, in my possession, one 4/4, H Clotelle violin in pristine condition for its age… with markings on the bridge piece which read, B. Wozny.” (Diana) I read it and before I even finished it, I , you know, I got so excited. And I was with a friend at the time, and she came running and she’s like what’s wrong, why are you screaming. (Masa) They agreed to meet the next day. (Diana) I was so nervous, just waiting for him to walk in the door and he did, and he’s carrying, my old, I could see my old ratty case.” (Kyle) And she stood up, an I walked up to her and I handed her the violin and I said to her, I believe this belongs to you. And she puts it down, she just looked at me and I could see the tear run down her face. (Kyle) And when she opened it, she just started to shake. (Diana) Ja, it was, it was incredible. You know I think especially now, we just dealing with so much, the world is in such a crazy place. Where it just feels like you are being bombarded with bad news. And it was just this incredibly sweet, and improbable, unlikely story. (Masa) It seemed fitting for Diana to take Viv back to see Bernard, the man whose signature had brought the violin home. (Bernard) It’s my pride,to,to, that she has the instrument and she’s young and healthy and that she can still perform. (Masa) Bernard says Viv’s return is a miracle. He’s still hoping that seven of his own violins, stolen years ago, will find their way home. (Kyle) I’d managed to bring a little bit of light into her life and I am glad I did. And it was never mine to begin, so it must go home to where she truly belongs. (Masa) And before I go, just enough time for a quick encore. (Masa) Bravo, bravo, I love it.

metadata.Summary: FINDING VIV On her tenth birthday, Diana Neille is given a violin by her father, a gift that carries weight long before its meaning is fully understood, because to raise a violinist is to endure years of unmelodious sound, the scrape of bow on string that can feel like chalk dragged across a school board, demanding patience before it offers anything like beauty in return. Diana practises, she plays in eisteddfods, and slowly, through the accumulation of hours and repetition, the violin settles into her body, becoming part of her muscle memory, something held instinctively between chin and shoulder, a physical extension through which her musical voice reaches the world. She names the violin Viv. Then, twelve years ago, Viv disappears, stolen during a house robbery at a moment when Diana’s life is already unsettled. At the police station, the charge office is full of people reporting hijackings, assaults and murders, and it feels almost impossible to explain that what has been taken is a violin, an object that is deeply personal but difficult to place alongside the violence surrounding it. Instead of persisting there, Diana turns elsewhere, appealing to a different kind of authority, the diffuse reach of the internet. She creates a Facebook page and writes that she has lost what feels like a limb, a violin she calls Viv, carefully listing every identifying detail she can remember. One detail matters more than the rest: the bridge was hand carved by her violin teacher and mentor, Bernard Wozny, a respected luthier who signs his bridges and stamps his name into the wood. And then she waits. Days turn into months, months into years, and eventually more than a decade passes with no response. Diana buys another violin, one that does the job but never quite feels right, its sound unfamiliar, its weight slightly off, and playing becomes effort rather than instinct. Over time, the sharpness of the loss fades, and Diana moves away from music making and into film making, carrying the memory of Viv quietly rather than actively. Recently, at supper, Diana’s niece tells her that she has started learning the violin, and Diana says she wishes she could have passed Viv down to her. If this were a piece of music, this would be the long pause, a rest held in the score. Not long after that pause, Diana receives a message from a stranger called Kyle, who says he thinks he may have her violin. At this point the story shifts, becoming a kind of whodunnit told in reverse. How did the violin survive? Where has it been all this time? Who handled it, and how did it make its way back? Kyle explains that while cataloguing his collection of instruments and music memorabilia, he noticed a name carved into a violin bridge. Curious, he searched it, and the old Facebook page appeared. He tells Diana that he bought a large collection of instruments from a friend who emigrated overseas, and that among them was this violin, which his friend had bought years earlier from a Cash Converters in Johannesburg, shortly after the original robbery. Kyle is an unlikely detective. Formerly a data analyst, now a devoted collector of musical objects, his tastes are eclectic rather than classical, his house filled with instruments and memorabilia gathered for love rather than profit. He meets Diana at a Woolworths, and when he walks in, he is carrying the case. Inside it is Viv. When the violin is found, Diana contacts her former teacher, Bernard Wozny, the man who carved and signed the bridge that ultimately solved the mystery. Bernard is now in his eighties, recently weakened by a stroke that has forced him to give up his workshop and pass his tools on to a younger luthier, Albertus Bakkes. There is another unresolved thread here too: Bernard’s own home was robbed not long ago, and several violins he had restored were stolen and never recovered. Viv is taken to see him. Bernard recognises the instrument immediately, not by its sound, but by the bridge. The question that remains is simple and unanswered: how many more stories like this are still sitting quietly in cases, waiting for the right detail to be noticed.
metadata.Further information: PEOPLE TO INTERVIEW Diana Neille – musician and filmmaker, owner of the stolen violin Kyle Fenton – the collector who identified and returned the instrument Bernard Wozny – violin teacher and luthier who carved and signed the bridge Albertus Bakkes – contemporary luthier now caring for the instrument and inheriting the tools and knowledge of the craft FORMAT AND STYLE A 10 to 12 minute Carte Blanche feature, structured as a gentle whodunnit, unfolding backwards through clues embedded in wood, memory and digital traces, led by narrative rather than exposition, with music and sound carrying the investigation forward.
